List of games with fantastic game writing, and I mean both literal in dialog and/or figurative gameplay:

Spec Ops the Line: it is Joseph Conrads "Heart of Darkness" in videogame form. It is written beautifully, and does psychological warfare better than most movies and books..

Thomas Was Alone: This game made me cry about quadraladerals. And that's not a joke. It is a superb example of how to write characters into a game, utilizing both witty and intelligent narration, and the actual gameplay mechanics to contextualize and characterize the players in the game

Bastion: Oh my god Bastion. How have more games not taken on this semi passive narrative style? Instead of being typical, and splitting game/narrative apart, large aspects of the narration are done whilst playing, with multiple well timed instances of contextual narration that can happen dependant on player gameplay.

Silent Hill 2: give it is voice acting faults, you can't deny that this game is stellarly written, with gameplay elements being more than just elements, and its many puzzles, riddles, and enemies being more than just "creepy" for the sake of being creepy.

Ace Combat 4 and 5: Now, I have a better understanding of 5 because its the one of the two games I actually have finished, but both are stellar examples of how to make a non polar conflict. As in you may be fighting an enemy, but the enemy isn't really evil, and that conflict effects both players, not just your side negatively.

Okami: Oh my god, Okami, this gem is one I wish more people recognize. It is a brilliantly done example of how to do the a fable. It has you as a player play as aspects of the Hero's journey in other character's stories. And that's what's important here, there is never just one story going on in Okami. Okami is a series of smaller, well directed narratives encompassed in your larger narrative being a god. And I think it is brilliantly excuted.

Papers Please: I would never have thought a game about pushing papers would ever even be a game worth making, but I'm glad that whoever did it did on their own. This game is not for everyone, and I will admit, it is boring. But there is a wealth of examples of how to do choice in games here that many people miss out on given its appearance. This game got me to stop and think about my actions, even if those actions had not long term consequences, or ones that could be on the scale of Mass Effects. I don't know how the man did it himeself, but Papers Please gets you to think what you will do in order to survive, and what you are willing to do to others. It is not happy, and it is not fun, and I love its existance.

Nier: now... this one is probably a bit of a stretch for some, but it is still an example I commend for its effort to be significant and try and stand out writing wise. I feel that over all, given all of its faults, the game struck quiet a few chords, and well overall a satisfyingly well written game. Its only for playstation and it certainly is a cult classic, but it is a game I appreciate exists even if it is a bit more specialized.

I think this strikes at the core of the issue - video games don't need a story. Pac-Man, Tetris, Space Invaders - all of the founding pillars of the industry have zero story and are all about game mechanics. If a game has good enough mechanics, you don't need any story at all. Modern examples of this being Guitar Hero and Mario Kart. Even games with decent attempts made at narrative would be fine without them if there was good enough gameplay - Far Cry 3 comes to mind there.

If you want story and are willing to sacrifice gameplay, then you're not looking for a game so much as a "narrative experience." The Telltale games are not really games - they're "choose your adventure" books where you walk around instead of flipping the page, and there are occasional quick time events thrown in to make it seem like a game.

People can enjoy what they want, but it would help to be mindful of the difference between playing a game and experience a narrative. The two are not inseparable.

Writing and story are similar, yet very different things. While the player can largely create their own story in open world games, the writing dictates the way the world reacts to the player and the way the player gains information from the game. Every thing you read is part of the game's writing. While it is true that not all games need story, ALL modern games(excluding the Candy Crush's of the world) do need good writing.

That said, an RPG doesn't have to chose between good writing or gameplay. The two are independent. Considering the massive budgets of modern games the only reason they have shit writing is that executives believe cheap creative writing grads are completely adequate.

I don't think that's very fair. In fact that is to assume that game narratives take away from a core experience. But the best games I've played were games where their core aspects related to their core narratives. It wasn't just "play the game, get a cutscene, get a story, move on" the best games portray their characters, narratives, stories, and themes directly through the gameplay itself.

I think its a little harsh to assume that games that focus soley on their mechanics and nothing else are definitvely always better than games that have a focus in narrative. It seems shallow in thought, and assumes that the gameplay will be significantly worse if time is spent on the narrative. It also suggests that the only thing videogames can provide are that, mechanics without depth of literary context. When in reality, in order to improve game narratives we have to get better at making the gameplay an aspect of the narrative, otherwise it will just feel like the narrative is, "another part of the game" instead of feeling integrated like it should be, and is when done correctly.

It also kind of assumes that videogames are designed with a set goal or purpose, and that the best ways have already been found. But in the words of Giorgio, "Once you free your mind about a concept of harmony and music being correct, you can do whatever you want. So, nobody told me what to do, and there was no preconception of what to do". This applies to all art mediums, and videogame designers need this ability to look past what their gameplay is expected to be if we are going to grow to have better narratives over all.

At this point, the video game industry is pretty much identical to the movie industry. And that includes the fact that the mainstream blockbusters are generally big, splashy, full of special effects and mostly stupid.

It's a function of budget and profitability. If you're going to spend tens of millions of dollars on a single game/movie, then the money managers are going to demand that, no matter what, it turns a profit. And when it comes to turning a guaranteed profit, appearance is more important than content. That's the number one priority - it has to look good, because that's all that many people will ever get out of it anyway. Any money spent on quality content will be entirely wasted on them anyway.

That means right off that you can generally cut corners a bit on content, and particularly on writing. You can do that because so many people don't value that, and if you can turn a profit on them, it doesn't matter how many people might point out that your movie/game is, at heart, stupid. And beyond that, and this is really the hell of it, you arguably should do that because making your movie/game too interesting and thought-provoking can alienate the core audience - the people who just respond to stuff that looks good. No matter what, you need to maintain your appeal to them, and if it's too complicated, they just won't bother with it. If you can push it a bit and make it actually sort of appealing and interesting without making it too complicated for them to understand, then you can appeal to an even wider audience, but that's a gamble, and a difficult one. It's hard to write so well that stupid people won't be confused AND smart people will be fascinated. It's easier (and cheaper) to just cut corners on the writing and stick with standard, drab, stupid pabulum that looks great. So that's what they do.

I think there are two primary reasons why the writing quality in AAA games is often pretty low: First, there is a huge amount of writing required most AAA games, and second, the writing is often a secondary (or tertiary) concern for the developers.

Super Mario Bros, which is arguably the first AAA game, had two written lines: "Thank you Mario! But our princess is in another castle!" and "Thank you Mario! Your quest is over. We present you a new quest." The rest of the story is contained in the instruction manual.

These days, every AAA game has several main characters, dozens of secondary characters, and hundreds of background characters, all with backstories and dialogue trees. On top of all that, there's the in-game text, which includes technical instructions and background information (e.g. library books, diary entries, ships' logs, etc.). Finally, there are the cutscenes and story structure (assuming the writers have a say in the overarching plot).

Skyrim has 60,000 lines of voiced dialogue. If each line is 8 words long (on average), that means Skyrim contains more words than the entire Lord of the Rings book series, just in dialogue alone. The game also contains 820 "books," which range in length but still comprise a massive amount of text. Writing a video game is a ton of work, and it's inevitable that some parts will be crappier than others. Of course, there's nothing preventing the developers from ensuring that all the text is awesome, but they would have to put a lot more resources and manpower into it, and most devs don't.

Developers have limited resources, so they have to allocate their budgets based on what matters most to consumers. Right now, consumers usually focus on gameplay and graphics over story, so the developers focus most of their efforts on those aspects. In any case, if consumers don't like the story, they can just skip it; they're stuck with everything else.

I'd like to see more effort put into stories, but it doesn't seem to be a high priority for developers right now.

I've recently played Mass Effect 1 to 3. Each one, individually, isn't a bad game. I actually enjoyed them, but in terms of story writing I did feel that 1 > 2 >> 3.

In the first one you're exploring an entirely new universe. Literally everything you see there is new. You're getting exposed to the many sentient species of the galaxy, learning how their social dynamics work, seeing different kinds of personalities, and so on. For the main quest, you're often visiting large hubs where you interact with many people, get a few quests to do on-spot before you move on to the actual action. In addition to that, in the citadel you're often presented with moments where your own crew talks to each other at the elevators, revealing how their relationship works. Apart from the other human crew members I really felt like I wanted to know everything about everyone in my party.

The main failure in the first one, is the planet exploration with the vehicles. You're often thrown in very large and open areas without any interesting features. For combing through a boring terrain you're rewarded with a few small through small and clearly templated dungeons. But that, in the game, is entirely optional.

The second one is working on an already-established universe. In order to present you to new things, it takes you on a trip through the "dark side" of the universe. While I felt the universe was suddenly crowded with edgelords, a share of them had actually pretty interesting background and stories. This one also gives you plenty of hubs where you're interacting with people and performing small quests locally before going to the main meat of the action.

My main problem with the second game is the excess of characters. Rather than really wanting to get to know each character like I did on the first game, I didn't actually care about a large share of the crew. I'll grant it probably took some caring to include all those characters, but more wasn't better. Also, Shepard for some reason starts behaving like an unreasonably horny person.

Now, the third game, that's one that seriously disappointed in the context of the Mass Effect trilogy. On its own it would have been a decent over-the-shoulder shooter, but in terms of delivering everything it promised it performed worse than a crooked politician.

The game reduces almost all crew interaction to a few moments in the ship, all hubs where you'd be talking to the various NPC characters in the galaxy have been removed, save for the citadel. Any character development seems infinitesimal save for the cringe romance plots. You're just jumping from one shooting section to another. The game barely shows you anything new about the universe, and whatever it does show, comes out sloppy or in unsatisfying quantities.

Also, it bothers me that the "rival" character looks like a weeabo in a shitty Mass Effect cosplay.

Now that my Mass Effect rant is over. Yes, I do get fed up with low quality of video game writing. Those that really bother me, though, are the games that promise a lot of content and excellent writing before fucking up. I'm fine with games that don't promise way more than they actually deliver.

The problem with any brilliant plan, any well thought out masterpiece or genius work of strategy, is it depends on something completely unexpected, unpredictable and unpreventable from not happening RIGHT at that moment. The best laid plans aren't undone by a clever counterattack, but by pure chance.

The head of MI5 briefed the Head of Defence on their findings hours, stating they had evidence the United States was bolstering the war on Ukraine from both sides AND using Dundee City as their main base of operations. The Head of Defence slammed his fist on the table in rage as he let out the rant he had been holding in for years; about the States blatant disrespect for their country. There had already been months of arguments over this situation, between the intelligence agencies and the Governments themselves, but this was the nail in the coffin. Britain's direct opposition of the States involvement in the matter was about to go public and there was no way the Head of Defence was backing down this time. He glanced across at the live video footage the MI5 head was showing, taken from inside Dundee police station itself as it showed a nervous administrator entering the room.

The administrator of the Dundee police station could only stare at the insanely large amount of weapons as it lay covered in tape and surrounded by military guards. Wondering what insanity could have caused such a pile of weaponry to be gathered, he worried about what he would do if this double check showed that there was, indeed, items missing. He prayed they were all still there.

The military guards stood idly, watching the guard fluster about after staring at the mass of weapons. As obvious as it was that this weapons stash needed someone to watch over it they still found themselves wondering why someone else couldn't do it. One of them gazed up at the security cameras above them and nodded before turning their gaze back to the wall opposite.

The security officer pushed himself up from the desk, satisfied that his staff would be able to keep an eye on the room. He was annoyed that he was unlikely to hear anything else about this case as it was already being passed higher up, and with the military there already there was a high chance he soon wouldn't have a pile of weapons to stare at. Moving back to his own desk he brought up the feed for the Camera #43 and wondered what the detective was asking the young boy.

The detective smiled as the young boy babbled on cheerfully about his latest project on Minecraft, the lad's mind apparently no longer interested in talking about the abandoned car he had found and now more interested in getting home before 'Dean ruins everything'. He himself however, could not get his mind off the find and was desperately trying to figure out what calamity had been prevented, hell maybe even started by the discovery of all these weapons. A gang war? An underground smuggling ring? A group of vigilantes? He was frustrated he had been taken off the case only hours into it, but his thoughts were cut short by the arrival of the boys mother.

The mother had been horrified when she had received the call from the police, and an order of magnitude worse when she heard that he was a witness to a potential murder case. They were unable to tell her more, making her feel worse still! She talked to Malcolm on the way back asking what he had been up to, if the police had been nice and if his day had been exciting. Trying to her best to act cheerful and as if nothing was wrong whilst she drove out into the country. Nodding along as Malcolm told her about him playing in the field and finding the crashed car. Biting her lip as Malcolm mentioned he had seen a man crouched over inside and the police had told him not to worry about it. Her mind was awash with thoughts as she pulled into Toby's house to buy strawberries and soon her worries drifted away as she talked to good ol' calm Toby. Toby laughed and commented he had crashed his car too, last week infact, yet sadly he wasnot part of a terrible murder scheme. Toby always made her laugh.

Toby waved the mother away, holding the smile. He walked into the shed and looked at the sheet covering his car, frightened to pull it back in case the ghost of the man he had killed burst through the window. His breathing accelerated as he remembered the feeling, turning the corner, than reaching across for his gloves, hearing the sound of brakes screeching and seeing the terrified look on the man's face as he plowed into the side of the man's car launching it off the road. He knew he should have called someone but he was so scared, he simply took off. It wasn't until he was several miles down the road he realised there was blood across his left seat and a man's arm lay next to him. He drove up one of the farming lanes his old mate Tim used and kicked the arm out, knowing fine well Tim's dogs would eat it before the day was done. At that point he saw the mobile phone, bloodied and jammed under the seat. He got back in the car as he panicked, thinking about the chance of it being tracked before having a brainwave! He found a stream running down towards the mighty river Tay and using a piece of rope from the back of the car, tied the phone to a stick. As he let it drift downstream he prayed that would be enough, driving off hoping that no-one would see him before he got home.

The mobile phone rang out a strange noise as it floated downstream. Calling out for it's now deceased owner. The deceased owner's hour of silence had ended and he hadn't checked in.

The FBI field operations agent paged up the information to his superiors immediately, as he failed to establish contact with the middle man for the transaction and he was already fearing that the worst had happened.

The Operations Officer quickly brought up the missions importance several levels as he demanded someone find out how someone knew about their Scottish agent and to get men on the scene as soon as possible. He cursed loudly as he stressed the importance of the deal and the potential conflict it could lead to with Ukraine and EU if the Russians were allowed free access across the border. If Scotland Yard got any idea of what they were pulling off in Dundee City then Great Britain would unleash a political firestorm unlike anything before. This could be not be discovered by MI5!

The dead man decided today really was a lovely day, and he needed a beautiful country photo before leaving. He didn't get to spend much time out in country when on missions like these so a quick dash up this road to the top of the hill would be wonderful. He would get a nice scenic shot for his wall when he got back, so he would call to check in as he rounded the corner an- SHIT!

If you look at the chart here based on "Time of Fall for an Average-Sized Adult in Stable Free Fall Position" (from "The Wild, Wonderful World of Parachutes and Parachuting" (Prentice-Hall, 1981), Bud Sellick ), you'll note that at 3 seconds a person would have fallen about 138 feet and would be travelling only 50 mph at that time. It takes about 3.5 seconds to reach 60mph (again according to that free-fall research). So based on this one particular source at least, Elon's claim of "Faster than Falling" acceleration seems to be accurate.

Edit: More maths! velocity at freefall = g * t
so if G (gravity on earth) = 9.8 m/s/s and Time = 2.8 seconds, then velocity of falling = 9.8 * 2.8 = 27.44 m/s = 61.38mph!
Based on these equations, a body at free-fall in earth's gravity would be traveling faster than 60mph after 2.8 seconds.

I know full body air resistance becomes a significant factor after about 20mph in my own testing (range testing of stand up electric scooters), so I presume that Elon must be calculating some air resistance in his claim.
